title: Adaptive admission batcher: sculpting prefill/decode batches to reduce tail latency
creator: Diego Morales
description:
Problem: Our continuous batching runner sees significant p95/p99 tail latency regressions under mixed workloads where short interactive decodes are delayed behind long prefill requests and deep-queued decode batches. This ticket implements an adaptive admission and batch-shaping layer that both (a) keeps latency-sensitive short requests moving and (b) maintains high GPU utilization for long-running prefill-heavy workloads.

Goals:
- Reduce p99 decode latency for 0-32 token decodes by >=40% under mixed workloads (measured at 95th and 99th percentile).
- Keep throughput loss <10% on sustained prefill-heavy offline jobs.
- Avoid excessive padding that increases token cost; target token-padding overhead <=8%.
- Provide operator knobs and realtime metrics so SRE and customers can tune admission policies per capacity tier.

Scope & Constraints:
- Implement admission control in the request router before sequence-length normalization and kernel selection. It must surface admission decisions to scheduling so kernel selection can prefer low-cost kernels for shaped batches.
- Integrate with existing KV cache fast-path: prioritize requests that hit KV cache to decode batches first when they are latency sensitive.
- Work must be compatible with Dedicated and Hosted runtimes; privacy-sensitive telemetry must not leak customer payloads.

Deliverables:
- Admission controller module (configurable token-budget, short-request priority, FIFO/Tail-drop variants).
- Batch shaper that groups by token-length bins and cache-hit/ miss to reduce padding while meeting SLO headroom.
- Integration tests + perf harness results comparing baseline to adaptive mode.
- Console dashboard panels showing admission queue length, shaped-batch composition, padding overhead, and p95/p99 by request class.
updates: 2026-02-26: Created ticket after postmortem from incident INC-2026-02-24 highlighted 120ms p99 spikes during mixed workload ramp on prod-east. Linked root cause to naive FIFO admission and all-or-nothing batching policies.

2026-03-01: Spike prototype implemented in branch feat/adaptive-admission. Prototype does fast path for short decodes (<32 tokens) and uses a token-budget counter per GPU; initial unit tests pass. (branch: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/tree/feat/adaptive-admission)

2026-03-04: Microbenchmarks on c6g-like test harness: p99 for short decodes improved from 480ms -> 280ms at 80% load, padding overhead increased from 3.1% -> 6.8%. Throughput for long prefills degraded by ~6%. Decided to proceed and add dynamic headroom tuning to meet throughput SLA.

2026-03-07: Design review with infra and SRE: agreed to expose three policy modes (aggressive-low-latency, balanced, throughput-first) and observable metrics. Agreed default for Hosted is 'balanced'. Added rollout plan with canary traffic at 10% capacity.

2026-03-10: Implemented batch-shaper that groups requests by (effective_length_bucket, kv_cache_hit) and emits shaped batches to the kernel scheduler with metadata tags used by kernel selection. PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2381

2026-03-12: Perf run on runtime-1.22 canary: observed p99 short-decode = 260ms (baseline 450ms), token-padding 7.2%, throughput drop 4.8%. Noted an edge-case where very bursty arrivals caused admission queue thrashing; added hysteresis to admission thresholds.

2026-03-14: Integration tests added to CI. Preparing canary rollout to prod-east with automated rollback if p99 increases >10% for any priority class. Draft console dashboard panels at: https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/abcd123/runtime-batching

Next steps: finish playbook for SRE (automatic knob tuning), complete Dedicated deployment validation, run customer workloads (query engine + chat) in staging, and ship release notes for runtime-1.22.
acceptance_criteria: p99 short-decoder latency reduced >=40% relative to baseline under mixed workloads in our standard perf harness
token-padding overhead <=8% on balanced policy and <=12% on low-latency policy
end-to-end throughput regression <=10% on prefill-heavy sustained jobs (30m window)
console exposes admission metrics and policy controls; canary rollout plan and automated rollback in place
unit + integration tests covering admission decisions, shaped-batch tagging, and kernel selection fallbacks
notes: Trade-offs discussed: aggressive low-latency policy will increase padding and cost per token; balanced policy selected as default to protect unit economics for most Hosted customers.

Kernel selection interplay: shaped batches tag the scheduler with 'likely-short' which biases selection toward lighter-weight attention kernels with better single-request latency; must ensure those kernels support the requested quantization path.
Security/Telemetry: admission bookkeeping only includes metadata (length bucket, cache-hit boolean, priority) — no customer prompt text is logged.
Fallback behavior: if admission backlog grows past a safety threshold, we fallback to time-window batching (max-wait 12ms) to avoid head-of-line starvation for long-running prefills.
